# Introduction  
## How Letters Become Words & How Tokens Represent All Languages

---

# Introduction

- English has only 26 letters.
- Yet English has hundreds of thousands to millions of words.
- LLMs use small vocabularies (8k–200k tokens).
- Tokens represent English and all world languages.

---

# English Alphabet: Only 26 Letters

- Lowercase: 26  
- Uppercase: 26  
- Punctuation/digits: ~40–50

English speakers:
- Understand: 20k–35k words  
- Use: 3k–5k actively  
- Dictionaries: 400k–600k  
- Total lexicon: 1–2+ million  

---

# How Do 26 Letters Produce Millions of Words?

### Key Morphology
- Concatenation: run + ning  
- Prefixes: un-, re-, anti-  
- Suffixes: -ing, -tion, -ize  
- Compound words: football  
- Borrowed words: French/Latin/Greek

---

# From Letters → Subwords → Words

LLMs use subwords, not words.

| Word | Subwords |
|------|----------|
| international | inter + national |
| unbelievable | un + believe + able |
| picklebally | pickle + ball + y |

---

# Why LLMs Don’t Need Huge Vocabularies

- English has millions of words  
- Tokenizers use only 8k–200k tokens  

Subwords:
- split rare words  
- compress common words  
- allow infinite combinations  
- represent all languages  

---

# Subword Example

::: {.no-code}
internationalization → inter + national + ization
:::

Tokenizers with 8k tokens can encode:
- English  
- all languages  
- slang  
- names  
- scientific terms  
- numbers/emojis  
- URLs  
- invented words  

---

# Vocabulary Sizes of Major LLMs

- GPT-2 / GPT-3 / NeoX: 50k  
- GPT-4 / GPT-4o: ~200k  
- LLaMA-1: 32k  
- LLaMA-2: 32k  
- LLaMA-3 / 3.1: 128k  
- Mistral / Mixtral: 32k  
- Gemma: 256k  
- Qwen: 152k  

---

# Bigger Vocabulary Pros/Cons

### Pros
- fewer splits  
- better multilingual  
- improved code/math  
- shorter sequences (faster)

### Cons
- sparse training  
- larger embedding matrix  
- harder optimization  

---

# Why Convert Text to Numbers?

::: {.no-code}
Text → Tokens → IDs → Embeddings → Tensors
:::

Neural networks operate only on numbers.

---

# Modeling Analogy

::: {.no-code}
(X1, X2, X3) → y

(token_{i-2}, token_{i-1}) → token_i
:::

---

# Static vs Dynamic Embeddings

**Static**  
- same vector everywhere  
- examples: TF-IDF, Word2Vec, GloVe  

**Dynamic**  
- vectors depend on context  
- used in GPT, BERT, LLaMA, Mistral  

---

# Static Embedding Example

::: {.no-code}
Word2Vec:
cat = [0.12, -0.89, 0.22]
dog = [0.15, -0.91, 0.25]
:::

Same vector in all contexts.

---

# Dynamic Embedding Example

::: {.no-code}
"The river bank overflowed." → bank_A
"I deposited money at the bank." → bank_B
:::

Meaning changes the vector.

---

# Tokenization Example

Sentence:  
I love large language models.

Tokens:  
I, love, large, language, models, .

IDs:  
[40, 3047, 4410, 6439, 7015, 13]

---

# Context Window (2 Tokens)

::: {.no-code}
[I, love] → large  
[love, large] → language  
[large, language] → models  
[language, models] → .
:::

---

# Embedding Example (Dim=3)

::: {.no-code}
40    → (0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
3047  → (-0.5, 0.1, 0.0)
4410  → (0.7, -0.2, 0.4)
6439  → (0.0, 0.3, 0.9)
7015  → (0.4, 0.4, 0.4)
13    → (-0.2, 0.0, 0.1)
:::

---

# Next Token Prediction

Model computes:

::: {.no-code}
P(next_token | context)

Example:
"large":     0.72  
"language":  0.10  
"models":    0.08  
:::

---

# Greedy vs Sampling

Greedy:  
choose the token with max probability

Sampling:  
draw token from the probability distribution

---

# Why Sampling?

::: {.no-code}
Sampling introduces variation → creativity.
:::

---

# Temperature

::: {.no-code}
Low T (0.1) → deterministic  
High T (1.0) → creative/chaotic  
:::

---

# Top-k vs Top-p

Top-k: keep top k tokens  
Top-p: keep the smallest set with cumulative probability ≥ p  

---

# Why LLM Predictions Differ

- sampling randomness  
- temperature  
- top-k / top-p  
- random seed  
- token-by-token amplification  

---

# Summary

- LLMs convert text → numbers  
- embeddings provide meaning  
- models predict next tokens  
- randomness = variation  
- same mechanics scale to trillion-token LLMs
